title: He Conceded a Point He'd Won. Then He Lost the Final He'd Earned. Kidambi Srikanth's Nine-Year Wait Goes On.
excerpt: The former world No. 1 reached the US Open badminton final in Fullerton, California, at 33 — and left with his fourth runner-up finish and one of the year's great acts of sportsmanship.
body:
Kidambi Srikanth did not win the US Open. But what he did in Fullerton, California, last weekend — across four bruising days of competition in one of the most Indian-American corners of the country — told you everything about where the 33-year-old is in his career. Still dangerous. Still proud. Still searching for the title that keeps slipping away.

The former world No. 1 reached the men's singles final of the BWF US Open Super 300 on Sunday, beating higher-ranked opponents along the way, including Malaysia's Lee Zii Jia in straight games in the round of 16. But in the summit clash against Chinese Taipei's Su Li Yang — nine years his junior and ranked 46th in the world — Srikanth's body could not keep pace with his ambition. He lost 15-21, 21-16, 9-21 in an hour and nine minutes.

It was his fourth final defeat at a BWF event, following runner-up finishes at the Syed Modi International, the Malaysia Masters, and the India Open. The title drought stretches back nine years.

The Final: A Second-Game Surge, Then Nothing Left

Su Li Yang was the sharper player from the start. The 24-year-old raced to a 10-5 lead in the opening game, deploying deceptive net shots and punishing Srikanth's returns with thunderous smashes. Srikanth clawed back to 10-10 — the crowd in Fullerton, filled with Indian-American fans who had driven in from across Southern California, briefly rose to its feet — but Su responded with seven consecutive points to take the first game 21-15.

The second game was different. Srikanth changed tempo, slowing the rallies and using his court craft to wrong-foot Su from the baseline. He surged from 15-13 to 20-13 in a stunning burst that carried the energy of a player who knows how rare these opportunities have become. He converted his fourth game point to level the match.

But the effort cost him everything. In the decider, Srikanth stayed with Su until 9-7. Then came an eight-point avalanche. Su took eight straight points to seal the match and claim his maiden BWF World Tour title. Srikanth could barely move in the final rallies, his legs heavy after a punishing semifinal the day before.

> "In the final game, we both were tired, so I told myself to keep the focus and keep pushing," Su said afterward."

"I can't believe I did it. In the final game, we both were tired, so I told myself to keep the focus and keep pushing," Su said afterward.

The Semifinal Moment That Defined the Tournament

More than the final, it was a single moment in the semifinal against Japan's Yudai Okimoto that will be remembered from Srikanth's run in Fullerton.

![Lee Zii Jia — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/eb/Lee_%26_Ng_President%27s_Cup_2023_%28cropped%29.jpg)

During a tense exchange, officials made what both players and spectators recognized as an incorrect line call. Protests followed. The officials would not reverse it. So Srikanth did something that badminton — or any sport — rarely sees at the professional level: he walked up to the referee and voluntarily conceded the point, handing it back to Okimoto.

The gesture drew widespread appreciation from fans, fellow players, and commentators. It was not a meaningless point in a blowout. The semifinal went to three tight games — 22-20, 15-21, 21-19 — and every point mattered. Srikanth won that match, but he did not win it by taking what was not his.

At 33, the Clock Ticks Louder

The arithmetic is unkind. Srikanth turned 33 in February. The players beating him in finals are increasingly from the generation that grew up watching him. When he won four Super Series titles in 2017 — including the French Open, Denmark Open, and Indonesia Open in the span of three months — he was the most feared singles player on tour. He reached world No. 1 in April 2018.

Since then, the titles have not come. Injuries, inconsistency, and the relentless churn of younger talent have kept him outside the winner's circle on the BWF tour. His last significant title was the Commonwealth Games gold in 2018. The wait has now stretched to nine years and counting.

But Fullerton was a reminder that the talent has not vanished. Beating Lee Zii Jia — a former All England champion and one of the most naturally gifted players in the sport — 21-14, 21-13 in the round of 16 was no fluke. Neither was fighting through a three-game quarterfinal against Jhuo-Fu Liao or surviving the semifinal against Okimoto.

What Comes Next: New Delhi Beckons

The BWF World Championships begin in New Delhi in August, less than 50 days away. India will host the biggest badminton tournament on earth at the Indira Gandhi Arena, and Srikanth — a former World Championships silver medallist — will want to be in the squad.

For Indian fans in the diaspora, the US Open was a bittersweet week. The tournament was held in Fullerton, deep in Orange County, where the Indian-American population has grown steadily over the past decade. Those who were in the arena saw a champion who could not quite close one more time but who showed, in one unforgettable act of sportsmanship, why sport still matters beyond trophies.

The title will come — or it will not. What Srikanth did in that semifinal chair will outlast whatever happens in New Delhi.
